findings.evidence: "If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee."
findings.fix: Rewrite as one sentence stating all three conditions must be met together, e.g., "The stipend is available only if the position is full-time, the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, and the request arrives before the benefit year ends."
findings.location: Eligibility section, the three "If…the stipend can apply" sentences
findings.violation: The first three sentences each independently assert that meeting that single condition makes the stipend "apply" (implying OR logic), but the fourth sentence then requires all three simultaneously (AND logic), directly contradicting the preceding sentences.

findings.evidence: "Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email."
findings.fix: Remove this sentence, or replace it with a general policy statement about backup-reviewer coverage during manager absences.
findings.violation: This describes a one-off operational incident (a specific manager traveling, a backup reviewer left uninformed) rather than a policy rule, and it is a confusing run-on sentence that doesn't belong in a reference policy document.

findings.evidence: "the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling" vs. "The request is reviewed within two business days."
findings.fix: Either state the two-business-day target as a goal with explicit exceptions for reviewer unavailability, or remove the conflicting narrative from How to Apply.
findings.location: How to Apply (manager traveling sentence) vs. Approval Timeline ("reviewed within two business days")
findings.violation: One section implies the review timeline can slip due to reviewer unavailability while the other states a firm two-business-day commitment, with no stated exception for this case.

findings.evidence: "The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist."
findings.fix: Clarify whether the checklist is mandatory or advisory, and rewrite in plain language consistent with the rest of the document.
findings.violation: This contradicts Approval Timeline's statement that "the manager confirms the equipment category matches the approved list," since "notwithstanding the standard review checklist" implies the checklist can be disregarded; the legalistic phrasing is also inconsistent with the plain-language tone used elsewhere.

findings.evidence: "Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time."
findings.fix: Rewrite as "The deposit reimburses costs the employee has already paid."
findings.violation: The sentence is filled with meaningless filler ("in order to," "at this point in time") that obscures a simple statement.

findings.evidence: "You must keep your equipment in good working condition and we may ask for a brief photo check once a year."
findings.fix: Rewrite in third person, e.g., "Employees must keep equipment in good working condition; the benefits team may request a photo check once a year."
findings.violation: This sentence switches to second-person "you/we" phrasing, breaking from the third-person voice ("the employee," "the manager") used everywhere else in the document.

findings.evidence: "Similarly, the policy applies to one device per category per employee."
findings.fix: Replace "Similarly" with "Additionally" or start a new, unconnected sentence.
findings.violation: "Similarly" implies this statement is analogous to the prior sentence about photo checks, but it is an unrelated rule about device limits, making the connector misleading.

findings.evidence: "You record the stipend item on the request form. Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month. Payroll releases the stipend item amount after that monthly review."
findings.fix: Use third person consistently and either define "stipend item" or replace it with the established term "stipend" / "equipment."
findings.violation: This again shifts to second-person voice inconsistent with the rest of the document, and introduces the undefined term "stipend item," which does not appear anywhere else in the policy.

findings.evidence: "Also, you submit the request in the portal. You track its status there until the payment clears."
findings.fix: Delete these sentences or consolidate portal-submission details into the How to Apply section only.
findings.violation: This duplicates information already given in How to Apply ("Employees start a stipend request in the benefits portal") without adding new content, creating redundancy.

findings.evidence: "Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt."
findings.fix: Merge this content into How to Apply near the beginning of the document, or expand it into a complete step list and remove the duplication.
findings.violation: This section duplicates and oversimplifies content already covered in How to Apply and Eligibility, and is placed near the end of the document after unrelated sections (Terminology Notes), making the overall structure incoherent.

findings.evidence: "The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period." compared to Program Overview's "The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter."
findings.fix: Remove this duplicate section or reconcile it with Program Overview so there is one consistent owner and cadence.
findings.location: Second "Overview" section (near the end of the document)
findings.violation: This is a duplicate "Overview" heading that contradicts the earlier Program Overview section on both who publishes the reimbursement log (benefits team vs. people operations office) and how often (after open enrollment vs. quarterly).

findings.evidence: "The team then routes the request to the correct approver based on department."
findings.fix: Reconcile the approval process into a single description of who approves requests and how they are routed.
findings.violation: This contradicts Approval Timeline, which describes "the manager" (not a department-based approver routed by the benefits team) as the sole reviewer, leaving it unclear who actually approves requests.

findings.evidence: "Once approved, the team schedules the reimbursement for the next pay cycle." compared to Reimbursement Amounts' "The finance office deposits the amount within one pay cycle."
findings.fix: Clarify in one place which team schedules versus which team deposits the reimbursement.
findings.violation: Two different sections attribute the reimbursement/deposit action to two different parties (the benefits team vs. the finance office) without explaining the division of responsibility.

findings.evidence: "The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out."
findings.fix: State explicitly how the finance review interacts with the two-business-day timeline (e.g., whether it runs concurrently or adds time).
findings.violation: This introduces an additional finance review step and a new $200 threshold that is never reconciled with the "reviewed within two business days" timeline in Approval Timeline, leaving the actual end-to-end timeline unclear for requests over $200.

findings.evidence: Heading "Questions and Updates" followed by "The benefits team publishes the vendor list each quarter. Every entry carries a date stamp so the record stays easy to audit."
findings.fix: Either rename the section to match its content (e.g., "Vendor List") or replace the content with actual guidance on how employees can ask questions or receive policy updates.
findings.location: Questions and Updates section (final section of the document)
findings.violation: The heading promises guidance on questions or policy updates, but the content only describes an unrelated, previously unmentioned "vendor list," with no contact information, FAQ, or update process.
